“Pleased to meet you proper, General,” Steiner said in a happy voice, offering a hand to the late forty-something ex-general.

De Vries only sighed. Still dressed as a general proper, he turned his attention out to the window. From his home on the island of Borkum, he could see the waters of the German Bight. After a string of failures compared to the massive success of Steiner, he could surmise why Steiner had visited him in the general’s own home

The AfD was dying. While at first they’d been met with success and enjoyed slow growth, it was clear to the General that the German people did not care for his reasonable solution. They cared more for the passionate Steiner, who stood there in front of him. Gustav Steiner, once public enemy number one, now quickly turning into a pop icon, turning heads from across the world. His face was known to most every European politician by now.

And de Vries? Who knew of him besides the army and the German right? He’d tried his hardest; he was a smart man, and educated man. But against a demon like Steiner, what could you do?

“Why have you come here?” Menno asked. He knew well the answer.

Though he couldn’t see it, de Vries was sure he could feel Steiner smiling that winning smile of his. “I want you to join me, Herr General.”

De Vries turned around. In a firm tone, he said, “I am no Nazi.”

“No, you are not,” Steiner went on without missing a beat. “You’re a moderate. You don’t go far enough, but even going as far as you would be a step in the right direction as far as Germany is concerned. I come to you with an offer, Herr General.”

Menno said nothing, just eyed Steiner. God, the man was tall and well-built. Those glacial blue eyes and that hair so blond it was almost white. He looked like the posterchild for the Aryan race. That thought made the general smile in amusement. Maybe Steiner was just born to be a Nazi?

“Work alongside me, Herr General, you and your party. Officially join up with the DNVP and become our ‘moderate’ wing. Betray none of your values, but merely join up with the bigger, rising star. It’s the only way for your values to get anywhere.”

“You mean to cannibalize us,” de Vries said. He looked to the his boots and the carpet underneath. Was this how the AfD ended? Was this how his career ended? Because Menno knew that if the AfD failed, the DNVP would be were its members would flock Perhaps it was inevitable.

“No. Work with us. Hand in hand, arm and arm. I do not ask that you betray your values. All I ask is that you join us. Together, Herr General, we can win—we can save Germany from the liars and thieves in charge who would do unto us harm.”

Menno swallowed. He glanced out the window once again. “And what of me? What of Maria Gottlieb?”

Steiner gave him a comforting look. “I would ask that you put your weight behind me. You campaign, and I campaign. I will put you into office. Maybe even make you President.”

At this, Menno cocked a brow.

“As for Maria, well, allow me to deal with her. She knows her way around public relations. And with me working with her, nothing could stop us. Our rhetoric is the one that Germans respond to, not yours anymore. I assure you, this is the best possible solution.”

Menno looked at the man and knew that, as awful as it was, Steiner was right.

“So,” Steiner said, offering a hand. “Partners?”

The General took a very long moment. He thought it over, considered his options. But in the end, nothing seemed to work.

With great hesitance, he took Steiner’s hand. The man had a powerful grip. “What choice do I have?”

And Steiner smiled wide.
